title: Project: Build, Deploy & Auto-Update a Live Website

sections.content:
## What You'll Build

By the end of this lesson you'll have:
- A real website live on the internet at `https://yourusername.github.io`
- A GitHub repository created from inside Claude Code — no browser needed for repo setup
- An AI-generated auto-deploy pipeline — every push to main automatically validates and deploys your site

This is the lesson where Git, GitHub MCP, and GitHub Actions stop being separate concepts and become one connected workflow. You built each piece individually. Now you use them together on a real project.

**What this lesson ties together:**
- **Claude Code** — builds the website files
- **GitHub MCP** (lesson 8-8) — creates the repo and pushes files without leaving Claude
- **GitHub Actions** (lesson 10-6) — AI generates the auto-deploy pipeline
- **GitHub Pages** — hosts your site for free, forever

You'll go from an empty folder to a live, automatically-deploying website in one session.

## Step 0 — Create Your GitHub Account (skip if you have one)

If you already set up GitHub in lesson 6-1, skip ahead to the main workshop.

**Create a free GitHub account:**
1. Go to **github.com** and click **Sign up**
2. Enter your email address
3. Create a password
4. **Choose your username carefully** — it becomes part of your website URL (`yourusername.github.io`). Use your real name or something professional you'll be comfortable sharing publicly
5. Verify your email when prompted
6. Choose the **Free** plan

**Set up a Personal Access Token for GitHub MCP:**
1. GitHub.com → your profile icon → **Settings**
2. Scroll to the bottom → **Developer settings**
3. **Personal access tokens** → **Tokens (classic)**
4. **Generate new token (classic)**
5. Name: `claude-mcp`, Expiration: 90 days, Scopes: tick `repo` and `workflow`
6. Click **Generate token** — copy it immediately, you cannot see it again
7. Add it to your Claude Code MCP config (see lesson 8-8 for the exact config path)

Once this is done, Claude Code can create repos, push files, and manage GitHub — all from chat.

sections.title: Project — Build, Deploy & Auto-Update a Live Website
sections.content:
Five phases. One session. A live website with automated deployment at the end.

---

## Phase 1 — Build the Website (15 min)

**Create a project folder and open it:**
```
mkdir C:\Users\YourName\Documents\my-website
cd C:\Users\YourName\Documents\my-website
code .
```

In the VS Code terminal, launch Claude Code:
```
claude
```

**Give Claude Code a complete brief:**
```
Build a clean, professional one-page website for me.

Name: [your name]
Tagline: [one sentence — who you are or what you're learning]
About: [2-3 sentences]
Links: GitHub (https://github.com/yourusername)

Requirements:
- Single index.html file, all CSS in a <style> block — no external files
- Dark background (#0d1117), white text, indigo (#6366f1) accents
- Minimal modern design — centered content, clean typography
- Mobile responsive
- No JavaScript, no CDN dependencies
- Under 50kb total
```

Preview it with Live Server (right-click index.html → Open with Live Server). Make any changes before moving on.

---

## Phase 2 — Create the Repo and Push via GitHub MCP (10 min)

You learned GitHub MCP in lesson 8-8. Now use it on a real task — creating and populating a live repo without leaving Claude.

**Create the repository:**
```
Using the GitHub MCP, create a new public repository named exactly:
yourusername.github.io

(Replace yourusername with my actual GitHub username: [your username])
Do not initialize it with a README.
```

Claude calls `create_repository` and the repo exists on GitHub instantly.

**Push your files:**
```
Now push my index.html file to the main branch of that repository.
Commit message: "Launch: built with Claude Code"
```

Claude calls `push_files` and your code is on GitHub.

**Verify:** Open `github.com/yourusername/yourusername.github.io` in a browser — you should see your file in the repo.

---

## Phase 3 — Enable GitHub Pages (5 min)

This part needs a quick browser visit:

1. In your repository on github.com, click **Settings**
2. Sidebar → **Pages**
3. Source: **Deploy from a branch**
4. Branch: **main** / folder: **/ (root)**
5. Click **Save**

GitHub will start building. In 2–3 minutes, go to: `https://yourusername.github.io`

Your site is live on the internet.

---

## Phase 4 — AI-Generated Auto-Deploy Pipeline (15 min)

Right now the site deploys automatically when you push to main — that's GitHub Pages' default. But there's no validation. You could push broken HTML and the world would see it.

Let's add a pipeline that checks your site before it goes live.

**Ask Claude Code to generate the workflow:**
```
Generate a GitHub Actions workflow for my website repository.
The workflow should:
1. Trigger on every push to main
2. Check the HTML is valid using htmlhint
3. Verify index.html is under 500kb
4. Output a deployment summary: file size, any warnings, and a link to the live site
5. Fail the pipeline (and block deployment notification) if HTML errors are found

Save it to .github/workflows/validate.yml
Explain what each section does as you write it.
```

Read every section Claude generates before accepting. If anything is unclear, ask: "What does this step do exactly?"

**Push the workflow file:**
```
Push the .github/workflows/validate.yml file to the repository.
Commit message: "ci: add HTML validation pipeline"
```

**Watch it run:**
1. Go to your repo on github.com
2. Click the **Actions** tab
3. Your pipeline is running
4. Click the run → expand each step

---

## Phase 5 — Make a Change and Watch It Deploy (10 min)

**Update the site via Claude Code:**
```
Change my website tagline to: [write something new]
Then push the updated index.html to GitHub.
Commit message: "content: update tagline"
```

**Back in the Actions tab:** a new pipeline run starts automatically. Watch it validate your HTML and report clean.

**Refresh `https://yourusername.github.io` after 2–3 minutes.**

Your change is live. This is the complete cycle: edit → push → validate → deploy. Every future update follows the same path automatically.

---

## What You've Built

| What | How |
|------|-----|
| Live website | GitHub Pages |
| Repo created | GitHub MCP from Claude Code |
| Files pushed | GitHub MCP — no git commands |
| Auto-validation pipeline | Claude Code generated the YAML |
| Future updates | Edit → ask Claude to push → pipeline runs → site updates |

Save your URL: `https://yourusername.github.io` — you'll use this repo again in the Part 21 capstone.

sections.title: Workshop A — GitHub MCP Repo Operations
sections.content:
Practice the full range of GitHub MCP operations — all from Claude Code chat.

**Step 1 — Create a test repo:**
Ask Claude Code: "Using GitHub MCP, create a private repository called 'mcp-practice' with the description 'Learning GitHub MCP from Claude Code'."

**Step 2 — Add files via MCP:**
Ask: "Add a file called NOTES.md to mcp-practice. The content should be today's date as a heading, and three bullet points about what I've learned in Part 10."

**Step 3 — Update an existing file:**
Ask: "Add a fourth bullet point to NOTES.md: what I still want to learn."

**Step 4 — Create an issue:**
Ask: "Create a GitHub issue in mcp-practice titled 'Add a projects section' with a description asking: what 3 fields should a projects section on a portfolio include?"

**Step 5 — Read state back:**
Ask: "List the open issues in mcp-practice and read me the content of NOTES.md."

**Reflect:** You created a repo, added and updated files, created issues, and read content — all from Claude's chat without touching a browser or terminal. What tasks in your actual work could this replace?

sections.title: Workshop B — Harden Your Deploy Pipeline
sections.content:
Extend your validation pipeline with additional checks suited to your site.

**Step 1 — Ask Claude Code what else is possible:**
```
For a static HTML website hosted on GitHub Pages, what are the most useful
additional checks I could add to a GitHub Actions validation pipeline?
List them ranked by value, with notes on whether each is free and how
complex it is to add.
```

**Step 2 — Pick 2 additional checks** from the list that match your site.

**Step 3 — Ask Claude Code to add them:**
"Add [check 1] and [check 2] to my .github/workflows/validate.yml. Push the updated file."

**Step 4 — Trigger a run** by pushing a small change to index.html.

**Step 5 — Security review:**
Ask Claude Code: "Review my validate.yml pipeline for security issues. Are there any steps where a malicious PR could abuse the workflow? Is GITHUB_TOKEN scoped correctly?"

Fix any issues it identifies before moving on.

sections.title: Workshop C — Deployment Notifications via GitHub Issues
sections.content:
Extend your pipeline to create a GitHub issue each time a deployment succeeds or fails — no external services required.

**Step 1 — Ask Claude Code to add notification steps:**
```
Extend my validate.yml to:
- On success: create a GitHub issue titled 'Deploy #[run_number] succeeded'
  with body showing: timestamp, file size, and the live site URL
- On failure: create an issue titled 'Deploy #[run_number] FAILED'
  with the error details and a link to the failed run

Use GITHUB_TOKEN only — no third-party services. Push the updated file.
```

**Step 2 — Trigger a test run** by pushing a change.

**Step 3 — Check the Issues tab** in your repo — did the issue appear?

**Step 4 — Ask Claude Code:** "Is creating a GitHub issue for every deployment a good long-term practice? What are the drawbacks, and what are the alternatives?"

**Step 5 — Decide:** keep the issue notification, switch to a different approach Claude suggested, or remove it entirely. Implement your decision.

sections.question: Your GitHub Actions pipeline fails: 'htmlhint: 3 errors found'. What is the correct next step?
options: Remove htmlhint from the pipeline — it's blocking deployment
Open the failed step's log, see what lines have errors, fix them locally, push again
Ignore it — GitHub Pages deploys regardless of Actions failures
sections.explanation: The pipeline failing means it caught a real problem in your HTML. The correct response: click the failed step in the Actions log to read the exact error lines, fix those issues in your local file, then push again — the pipeline will re-run and pass. Removing the check eliminates your safety net. GitHub Pages does deploy regardless of Actions failures (they're separate systems), which is exactly why validation matters — without it, broken HTML goes live silently.

sections.question: What is the key difference between pushing files via GitHub MCP versus using 'git push' in the terminal?
options: MCP uses the GitHub API to update files directly — no local git history or branches. git push creates a proper commit with full history, author, and supports branching and rollback
They are identical — MCP is a git wrapper
MCP only works for files under 1MB
sections.explanation: GitHub MCP's push_files calls the GitHub Contents API — it creates or replaces files on GitHub with a commit, but you have no local git repository tracking the history. With git push, you have a full local history (git log, git diff, git revert, branches). For a real project you'd use local git for version control and branching, and use MCP for quick operations or automation. The right tool depends on the task: local git for development workflows, MCP for programmatic file management from Claude.

sections.content: **Lesson 10-8 complete.** You have a live website, a GitHub repo managed from Claude Code via MCP, and an AI-generated pipeline that validates every push. This is the complete modern deployment workflow — the same pattern professional teams use, available to one person with free tools. The Part 21 capstone returns to this site and adds portfolio depth, custom domain setup, and analytics.
